title: Why JD Vance Invoked Huey Long
author: Adam Rowe
content:
![Why JD Vance Invoked Huey
Long](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/08/AP081016011116.jpg)

Vice President JD Vance made headlines last week by favorably quoting Huey
Long, the Depression-era senator and governor of Louisiana. "The great
Southern populist," Vance said, made "'every man a king' the goal of his
political program." The Trump Administration shares that goal, Vance implied.
"But no man is a king if their castle is under siege by criminals," the vice
president continued. "No man is a king if they can't take their family out to
dinner without being mugged or having their car jacked."

Physical safety for all citizens was not quite the limit of Long's ambitions.
The Southern demagogue railed against the rich as the sole cause of poverty
and championed a massive wealth distribution program. On economic policy, he
was much closer to the DSA than to Trump's GOP.

> "He was much closer to the DSA than to Trump's GOP."

But in American politics, substance runs a distant second to style. Among the
overeducated, underemployed professionals calling themselves Democratic
Socialists, Long's cornpone act would have as much appeal as a can of cheese
whiz. Trump's warmest admirers and worst enemies, on the other hand, will
recognize the president's resemblance to Huey Long.

In the famous Tennessee Williams play "A Streetcar Named Desire," Stanley
Kowalski (played by Marlon Brando) sits sulking at the dinner table as his
wife and sister-in-law comment on his boorish manners. Told to clean himself
up, he lashes out, smashing glass plates with his fist and throwing them
against the floor and the wall. "Just remember what Huey Long said," Kowalski
snarls as his wife and sister-in-law, Blanche DuBois, stare down at the table,
trembling in terror, "that every man is a king and I'm a king around here and
don't you forget it!"

Kowalski--brutish, ignorant, belligerent with insecurities he converts into
grievances, smashing up his own house to show he's king within it--is the
progressives' image of a MAGA voter in every respect save Brando's sex appeal;
Blanche--a snob, a fraud, delusional, wilting and helpless--is MAGA's idea of
a twenty-first century progressive. As these two political archetypes battle
and bring out the worst in one another, it was fitting for Vance to remind us
all again of Huey Long.
